Clinical history (case record; may contain prior observations):
age: 35
gender: male
history: A 35-year-old male, post-ironman, presented with severe dyspnoea, 80% O2 saturation, haemoptysis, and tachypnoea. Developed nausea and vomiting during cycling and walked the last 20 km of the marathon due to fatigue. Mild COVID-19 three weeks prior. He was admitted to the ICU with severe respiratory distress.

Experience from other cases; may not apply. Check against the current original images; these are not answers for this patient.

symmetric bilateral enlargement strongly favors sarcoidosis over unilateral processes like tuberculosis or lymphoma.", "Examine the lung parenchyma for perilymphatic micronodules or clusters of nodules surrounding a central mass (sarcoid galaxy sign), which are specific to sarcoidosis.", "Verify the absence of pleural effusions (rules out heart failure) and cavitation (rules out abscesses/TB) to confirm the diagnosis."]}]

Based on the progression of the chest X-rays, which diagnosis is most consistent with the observed imaging findings and clinical history of the patient, particularly in Figure 3, and why?
A) Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), due to persistent bilateral alveolar infiltrates.
B) Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, indicated by bilateral infiltrates and heart enlargement.
C) Pneumonia, due to localized consolidations and bilateral involvement.
D) Exercise-induced pulmonary haemorrhage (EIPH), due to diffuse alveolar damage consistent with intense physical exertion.
E) Pulmonary embolism, because of lack of significant resolution in infiltrates.
F) Viral pneumonia, given the history of recent mild COVID-19 infection.
